paragraphs: Swamiji once told of a rich man in Rome who discovered one day that he had only about a million pounds left. Wondering what he would do tomorrow, he killed himself on the spot. To him, a million pounds felt like poverty.

So what is joy, and what is sorrow? Swamiji said both keep shifting and vanishing. As a small boy he had believed that being a cab driver, driving around all day, would be the height of happiness. He no longer thought so. Everyone's idea of pleasure is different. He had met a man who could not be happy without swallowing a lump of opium every day, and who imagined heaven as a land made of opium. That, Swamiji joked, would be a very bad heaven for him.

Arabian poetry, he noted, keeps describing paradise as beautiful gardens with rivers flowing through them, which makes sense for people from a dry land. But Swamiji had spent much of his life in a country with too much water, where floods swallowed villages and took thousands of lives every year. His heaven would have no rivers at all; it would be a place where very little rain fell.

Our pleasures keep changing as we change. A young man pictures heaven with a beautiful wife; as an old man he no longer wants one. What we call heaven, Swamiji concluded, is shaped by what we lack, and it changes as our needs change. Understanding this is one of the hardest lessons, and one of the last illusions we let go of.
learn: The thing you are sure will make you happy right now, a gadget, a rank or a relationship, may mean little to you in five years. Notice how your wants keep shifting, and do not stake your whole peace of mind on any of them.
